chunks: "Any pair of input voltages can be split into a differential part, which is the difference between them, and a common-mode part, which is their average.
A good differential amplifier amplifies the difference by A d and ignores the common part, so V out equals A dV d plus A cmV cm .
The ideal values are that A d is large for an open-loop op-amp, or whatever I design for in a closed-loop circuit, say 10, and A cm is exactly zero.
So the ratio, the common-mode rejection ratio A d over A cm , is infinite. In real hardware A cm isn't zero.
In a difference amplifier built from four resistors, a mismatch makes the two input paths have slightly different gains, so part of the common-mode voltage leaks to the output.
With 1% resistors and a gain of 10, the worst case CMRR is only about 275, or 49 decibels.
That means 1 volts of common-mode noise produces about 37 millivolts at the output, bigger than the signal from a 1 millivolts differential input.
Real op-amps are specified at 80 to 120 decibels CMRR, but the surrounding resistors usually dominate, which is why instrumentation amps use laser-trimmed matched resistor networks."
